sentences.text: Leedsichthys was an extinct fish belonging to the pachycormid lineage that inhabited oceans during the Middle and Late Jurassic periods.
Much of the animal's body was made of cartilage, a tissue type that rarely preserves well in the fossil record.
Over seventy individuals have been discovered, yet most of these remains are partial and lack teeth.
Instead of teeth, the fish possessed gill rakers measuring between three and twelve centimeters long with small structures pointing obliquely forward and upward.
This species holds the record for being the largest known member of the bony fish group.
A crocodile tooth found inside a Leedsichthys bone suggests the fish was scavenged after death rather than eaten while alive.
Arthur Smith Woodward formally described the genus in 1889, naming it after the British collector Alfred Nicholson Leeds.
On August 22, 1888, Othniel Charles Marsh determined that the fossils collected by Leeds were actually skull bones of a giant fish instead of dinosaur armor.
Remains of this fish have been recovered from locations including England, France, Germany, Argentina, and Chile.
Leedsichthys functioned as a suspension feeder, using specialized gill rakers to filter zooplankton and small animals from the water.
Scientists are still unsure whether algae or phytoplankton were also part of its diet.
Comparisons with modern teleost fish indicate the animal could swim at speeds of 17.8 kilometers per hour while keeping its oxygen supply stable.
Growth rings in the bones suggest it took twenty-one to twenty-five years to reach adulthood, and a 2013 study proposed this growth was slow and nearly linear.
However, a 1993 French study argued that the bone structure pointed to a high metabolic rate instead.
The pliosaurid Liopleurodon was an apex predator in the Oxford Clay seas capable of attacking Leedsichthys.
The type species for the genus is Leedsichthys problematicus.
Arthur Smith Woodward initially placed the fish in the Acipenseroidea, grouping it with sturgeons.
It is now viewed as the start of a lineage of large pachycormid suspension feeders that persisted until the Late Cretaceous, showing convergent evolution with baleen whales.

Fossils range from the Callovian to the Tithonian stages and have been found in the Callovian of England and northern Germany, the Oxfordian of Chile, and the Callovian and upper Kimmeridgian of France.
There is an ongoing debate regarding whether Pachycormidae, including Leedsichthys, are basal Teleostei or members of a separate order Pachycormiformes sister to Teleostei.
Scientific opinion is divided on the size of the animal, with Liston arguing for much lower length estimates than earlier popular accounts.

In 1999, Martill suggested that climate change at the end of the Callovian caused extinction in northern seas, but Liston argued against this in 2010 by noting fossils from the Kimmeridgian in Normandy.
